final_message:
The four 128-bit kernels (`filter_i128`, `count_i128`, `sum_i128`, `minmax_i128`) are in all three variants, and `make -C native-kernels test` reports `20/20 kernels PASS` for each variant, both natively and under ASan/UBSan. Everything is committed and the working tree is clean.

**What was built** (new code appended to the end of each existing `.S` file; the original 16 kernels are untouched):
- **`x86_scalar`**: plain integer code. Filter and count compare one row at a time and collect results into a 64-row mask. `sum_i128` keeps a 192-bit running total, so it is always exact. `minmax_i128` does one range check per row and updates only when a value falls outside the current min/max.
- **`x86_avx2`**: compares 4 rows per step. `sum_i128` splits each 64-bit word into halves so the vector lanes stay exact, then folds them into a 192-bit total. `minmax_i128` skips the update step when no lane needs it.
- **`x86_avx512`** (optional, and the default on this machine): 8 rows per step using mask registers and unsigned compares; the sum uses the same exact method as AVX2. Min/max never branches on the data.
- **Overflow detection** works the same way everywhere: the sum is `PQK_OVERFLOW` exactly when the final 192-bit total doesn't fit in int128. So an overflow in the middle that cancels out is fine, and any final sum out of range is always reported.
- Every new kernel's header comment covers register usage, the algorithm and (for the sum) how exact overflow detection works.

**Extra testing:** I extended the checks in `verify/`; all pass for all three variants:
- reads and writes stopping exactly at protected memory pages (including `a`, `b` and every output);
- 300,001-row extreme columns, and 2,000 sums landing exactly on `INT128_MAX`/`INT128_MIN` (must pass) or one past them (must overflow);
- register and stack preservation (ABI);
- a build with tiny sum chunks so the folding code runs constantly.

I also deliberately broke a copy of the scalar overflow check, and the new tests caught it.

**Measured speedups** vs the C reference (64 MB column, ns per row):

| kernel | L3-resident: scalar / AVX2 / AVX-512 | from DRAM: scalar / AVX2 / AVX-512 |
|---|---|---|
| filter_i128 | 3.2× / 4.1× / 5.7× | 2.6× / 2.8× / 3.1× |
| count_i128 | 2.1× / 3.1× / 3.0× | 1.7× / 1.8× / 1.8× |
| sum_i128 | 1.8× / 2.6× / 2.7× | 1.3× / 1.4× / 1.5× |
| minmax_i128 | 1.8× / 4.0× / 3.7× | 1.6× / 2.4× / 2.4× |

The official unpinned `make bench` run landed on the slower-memory half of the chip and matches the DRAM column. The full tables, tuning experiments and design notes are in `native-kernels/x86_64/README.md`.

**Limitations:**
- The scalar `minmax_i128` slows down on unfavourable data (steadily increasing values, or frequent unpredictable new extremes). It then runs at roughly reference speed, about 0.8–0.96 ns/row.
- AVX-512 only matches AVX2 for count, sum and min/max; it is clearly faster only for filter.
- From DRAM the benchmark program reaches only about 50 GB/s on these kernels, against about 72 GB/s for the same kernel in my own test harness. I attribute that gap to how the benchmark process places memory, not to the kernels, but I didn't confirm the cause.
- All numbers come from this one AMD Zen 5 machine.
